steps.action:
# The Last Light

Old Maren had kept the light for thirty-one years, long enough that the rhythm of it had replaced her heartbeat. Wind up the mechanism. Trim the wick. Polish the lens until the Fresnel glass caught even the weakest afternoon sun and threw it back doubled.

She had outlasted three marriages — two of other people, one of her own — and a hundred storms that the mainland newspapers called catastrophic. From her tower, catastrophic just looked like weather.

The supply boat came on Tuesdays, when it came at all. The young man who piloted it, Henrik, always seemed faintly sorry for her. He would hand up the crates with an expression like he was delivering meals to a prisoner.

"Don't you get lonely?" he asked one Tuesday in October, the harbor behind him going copper in the late light.

Maren thought about the seals that barked on the eastern rocks every morning. She thought about the freighter captain who always answered her radio check with "Good evening, Maren" in a voice like warm bread, though she had never seen his face. She thought about the way a storm looked from inside the eye of it — orderly, almost polite, the chaos arranged neatly in a circle around you.

"Ships don't ask me that," she said, and took her crates inside.

That night a fishing vessel came through the channel in zero visibility, feeling its way through fog so thick it had weight. Maren didn't know its name or how many people were aboard. She just kept the light turning.

That was the whole job. That was enough.
